title: From Tripods to Bipods Reducing the Queue Number of Planar Graphs Costs Just One Leg

predicted_errors.error_location: Definition 3.2 (property P2.b) vs. Section 2 description of bipods and the construction in the proof of Theorem 3.4
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Definition 3.2 states that the paths are P1=(u_{s_u},...,u_{t_u}), P2=(v_{s_v},...,v_{t_v}) with u_i,v_i in L_i, and requires '(u_{s_u}, v_{s_v}) ∈ E', i.e., the two endpoints in the SHALLOWEST BFS layers must be adjacent. However, Section 2 describes a bipod as 'an edge e incident to two vertical paths of e' where the paths go upward from e, and in the proof of Theorem 3.4 the bag is built from the two tree paths running from the triangle/edge endpoints v1,v2 (deepest vertices, joined by the edge (v1,v2)) up to their ancestors p1,p2 (shallowest vertices, which are NOT adjacent to each other). Hence the constructed bags satisfy an adjacency at the deep ends (u_{t_u},v_{t_v}), contradicting condition P2.b as stated.

predicted_errors.error_location: Proof of Theorem 3.4, triangular and quadrangular iterative steps (application of Lemma 3.3)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The proof claims: 'If B_{x_{k+1}} is not acyclic, by Lemma 3.3 we can find a subset of B_{x_{k+1}} inducing an acyclic bipod such that p1 and p2 are connected via a path through that bipod.' But Lemma 3.3 truncates the paths from the small-index (shallow-layer) end: it returns P1'=(u_i,...,u_{t_u}) and P2'=(v_j,...,v_{t_v}) with i ≥ s_u, j ≥ s_v, i.e., it deletes exactly the vertices nearest to the roots p1 and p2. Consequently the truncated bipod need no longer contain neighbours of p1 and p2, so neither the claimed connection of p1 and p2 nor the required adjacency of the new bag to B_{x_1} and B_{x_2} (needed for Invariant I3.4.6 and the goal stated before the case distinction) follows.

predicted_errors.error_location: Proof of Theorem 3.4, quadrangular iterative step (definition of edges e_2 and e_4)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text reads: 'if there is an edge e_2 = (v_{k+1}, v_2), where v_{k+1} ∈ B_{x_{k+1}} and v_2 ∈ B_{x_3}, we also connect x_{k+1} to x_2. Similarly, if there is an edge e_4 = (v_{k+1}, v_2), where v_{k+1} ∈ B_{x_{k+1}} and v_2 ∈ B_{x_3}, we also connect x_{k+1} to x_2.' Both conditions are identical and both refer to B_{x_3}; e_2 must be an edge to a vertex of B_{x_2} and e_4 must be an edge to a vertex of B_{x_4} (connecting x_{k+1} to x_4), as is clear from the subsequent discussion of cycles C_{143}, C_{14}, C_{43} and faces f_{14}, f_{43}.

'By Invariant I3.4.5, we have t_1 ∈ L_{i_1}, t_2 ∈ L_{i_2} and t_3 ∈ L_{i_3} such that i_2 ≥ i_3 and i_2 ≥ i_1.' Invariant I3.4.5 only concerns membership of unassigned vertices in subtrees of T rooted at bag vertices; it says nothing about the relative BFS layers of the three vertices of the triangle t, and there is no reason why the layer of t_2 should be the maximum among the three. The subsequent argument ('t_1 the vertex of t on the lowest layer', placement of v_y in L_{i_1+1}) depends on this unsupported assertion.
'already inspired a plethora of follow-up works [7, 10, 14, 18, ?, 24, 27, 29, 30]' contains an unresolved citation key ('?'), i.e., a broken/missing reference in the bibliography list.

The path is defined as P = (p_1, p_2, ..., p_d) for d the largest index with L_d ≠ ∅, but the construction then uses vertices p_i for every layer i ∈ {0, ..., d} (e.g. '((v_1, p_i), x)' for i = 0,...,d and the bipartite connections between layers i and i+1). The path must therefore have d+1 vertices p_0,...,p_d; as written the indices do not match the layering.
